overview: This single-page file register, headed “Antropology in Taiwan,” records one paper originating in Taihoku (modern Taipei) and dated January 21, 1936. Its synopsis concerns Paul K. Benedict’s proposed anthropological research in colonial Taiwan, for which permission was not granted, and also refers—through badly corrupted OCR—to preliminary reports involving members of a second psychological-project expedition. The underlying report or despatch itself is not present in the supplied file text.

subfiles.summary: The sole entry records a paper numbered 1, apparently associated with Taihoku and dated January 21, 1936. It states that Paul K. Benedict was not granted permission to pursue his proposed research. A final, severely corrupted passage mentions preliminary reports and several members of a second psychological-project expedition, but its precise wording and judgment cannot be recovered reliably from the OCR.

interest: The sheet is useful evidence of official control over foreign anthropological fieldwork in Japanese-ruled Taiwan and identifies a denied research proposal by Paul K. Benedict early in his career. Because only the file register survives in the supplied text, it also illustrates how archival control documents can preserve the subject and disposition of a missing report. The damaged reference to an additional psychological-project expedition may point to a wider network of research activity, although the OCR is too uncertain to identify it confidently.
